1:
What occasion produced the psalm nobody settles. John Calvin thinks it thanksgiving for a particular deliverance rather than for God’s constant protection, Jerusalem having been preserved in extreme danger contrary to all expectation; some refer it to the raising of Sennacherib’s siege and others to Jehoshaphat’s victory, but it cannot be ascertained, and the poem seems rather the language of faith under threat than of triumph over a vanquished foe. Adam Clarke canvasses more: Calmet supposed it composed by the sons of Korah on their return from Babylon, the disturbances being those in the Persian empire after Cambyses died and the Magi usurped the government; Houbigant made it an earthquake on the night Sennacherib’s army was destroyed.

The title is disputed in the same way. Adam Clarke renders it an ode upon Alamoth, or concerning the virgins, possibly a choir of singing girls; some translate the word secrets or mysteries, and Kennicott took it for an instrument. John Calvin narrows it to two, an instrument or the opening words of some well-known song, and prefers the second. Augustine of Hippo takes the reading for things secret and makes it the door into the psalm: secret it is, but he who was crucified at Calvary has rent the veil so that the secrets of the temple might be discovered, and since the cross was a key by which closed things might be opened, we may trust that he will be with us and these secrets revealed.

On the opening claim they are agreed and emphatic. C.H. Spurgeon takes it as a rejection of the alternatives: not our armies or our fortresses, for others may vaunt impregnable castles and gates of iron, but God is a far better refuge, and stands his people in better stead than legions. He presses the possessive — make sure of your own portion in God — and the tense, God being our refuge just now, as truly as when the words were penned. Matthew Henry divides the verse by our conditions: are we pursued, God is a refuge to flee to, and we may think ourselves secure on good grounds, as at Proverbs 18:10; are we oppressed, he is our strength to bear us up. The help he calls a help found, one we have proved; or a help at hand; or a help sufficient for every case. Charles Ellicott would render the pair a sure stronghold, as in Luther’s hymn, and the last phrase often found a help. John Gill makes the refuge Christ himself, typified by the cities of refuge under the law.

Whether the upheaval of the next verses is literal is the last question. Charles Ellicott renders the first clause at the changing of the earth and thinks the psalmist had in mind the sudden convulsion of an earthquake — travellers, he notes, all remark on the signs of tremendous volcanic agency in Palestine. He figures Israel fearless amid tottering kingdoms, comparing the heathen poet on the fearlessness supplied by virtue. Of the next verse he admires the conciseness of the original, they roar, they foam, its waters, setting Homer’s three-word ocean beside it; the change of construction, he adds, suggests the refrain has dropped away. Adam Clarke reads it politically: the earthquake means political commotion, by mountains kings or secular states may be intended, and waters in prophetic language signify peoples in commotion. This people had seen all Asia at war and Babylon sacked by the Persians, while Cyrus behaved as a father to them. John Wesley keeps to the figure: though there should be nothing but confusion and desolation round about us, often expressed by such metaphors. John Gill observes only that such a noise makes men’s hearts fail for fear, and that the saints have no reason to fear men or devils, nor to indulge a slavish fear on any account, since the Lord is on their side.
4:
Whether the river is a real watercourse is the first question, and Charles Ellicott settles half of it philologically. The Hebrew word means a perennial stream, as distinguished from the term for a torrent bed dry except in the rainy season; the Kidron is therefore plainly not alluded to. Many think Siloam intended, and he refers to Stanley and to Isaiah 12:3 and Ezekiel 47:1; but there may be no local allusion at all. The river flowing calmly along may be only a symbol of the peace and blessing of the divine presence, as the tumult of the sea in the previous verse is of the world’s noisy troubles — and the Greek seems to connect this river with the waters of the verse before. John Gill allows the local reading Ellicott rejects, the Kidron or the waters of Shiloah which supplied the several parts of the city, but takes the words figuratively as applicable to gospel times. The river may be the gospel, whose streams are its doctrines; or the Spirit and his graces; or the Lord himself, a place of broad rivers to his people; or rather, he thinks, God’s everlasting love, whose head is the heart of God, whose channel is Christ Jesus, and whose rise was in eternity.

John Wesley keeps it short: the river designs the gracious presence and blessing of the Lord, often described under the name of waters, and shall not barely preserve the city from danger but give great occasion for thanksgiving. C.H. Spurgeon makes it divine grace, a never-failing river, the river of the water of life of which the church above as well as below partakes. It is no boisterous ocean but a placid stream, not stayed by earthquakes or crumbling mountains; its streams are not transient like Cherith, nor muddy like the Nile, nor furious like Kishon, nor treacherous like Job’s deceitful brooks, but clear, cool and gladdening.

He then gives the image a military point. The great fear of an Eastern city in war was that the water supply should be cut off during a siege, since if that were secured the place could hold out indefinitely; and Jerusalem, standing for the church, is described as well supplied, to set forth that in seasons of trial all-sufficient grace will be given to enable us to endure. The church is a well-ordered city, walled with truth and justice, garrisoned by omnipotence, whose burgesses live in the smile of the King.

Adam Clarke takes the verse in a direction no one else follows. He reports the Chaldee, which understands the river and its divisions as the peoples who should be converted and so make Jerusalem glad by flowing together to the worship of the true God; but he thinks it may rather be the vast Medo-Persian army and its divisions — the branches which took Babylon and which, instead of destroying the poor Jews, preserved them alive and gave them liberty, so that the city of God was gladdened.

On the promise that follows they are agreed. John Gill distinguishes the presence meant: not merely by essence, power and providence, as God is in the midst of the world, but by his gracious presence, which always continues though not always perceived, and is a sufficient antidote against all fear of men and devils. Adam Clarke reads it as a pledge that God will not abandon those who trust in him but will maintain his own cause, and that if his church is attacked he will help her with the utmost speed. The last words he explains by the figure they contain — as by daybreak the shadows are dissipated, so by the bright rising of Jehovah the darkness of adversity shall be scattered. Charles Ellicott gives the same phrase its literal sense, at the turning of the morning, evidently metaphorical of the dawn of a brighter day.
6:
Matthew Henry makes these verses glory given to God both as King of nations and as King of saints. As King of nations he rules the world by his power and providence and overrules all the affairs of men to his own glory, doing according to his will among the inhabitants of the earth, so that none may say to him, what doest thou? The first proof is here: he checks the rage and breaks the power of the nations that oppose his interests in the world. The heathen raged at David’s coming to the throne and at the setting up of the kingdom of the Son of David, as at Psalm 2:1; the kingdoms rose in a tumultuous furious manner to oppose it, but God uttered his voice, spoke to them in his wrath, and they were moved in quite another sense — struck into confusion, all their measures broken, so that the earth itself melted under them and they found no firm footing. Their earthly hearts failed them for fear and dissolved like snow before the sun, a melting of the spirits of enemies such as is described at Judges 5:4 and at Luke 21:26.

John Wesley reduces the movement to three glosses: they raged against God and his people; he spake to them in his wrath; the inhabitants of the earth were consumed. Adam Clarke keeps the history in view. There had been terrible wars on all hands and mighty states were crushed, while the poor Jews were kept in peace by the especial favour of God: kingdoms were moved while they were preserved. As for the voice, the words seem to him to refer to thunder, lightning and earthquake, though they may equally be figurative and point to the wars already mentioned — God gave the command, and one empire was cast down and another raised up.

John Gill carries the raging forward through church history. The heathen raged as at Christ’s first coming, against him and his gospel and his people, and continued so through the first three centuries; then the pagan kingdoms of the Roman empire were removed. Since then another sort of heathen, the Papists, have raged in violent persecutions and in the bloodshed of the martyrs, and will rage again at the downfall of Babylon.

Charles Ellicott, alone among them, reads the verse as workmanship rather than history. The absence of conjunctions, he observes, and the sudden change from the preterite to the future lend a vividness to the picture, which he sets out in the broken lines it makes: raged heathen, tottered kingdoms; gave with his voice the signal; and, lo, melts the earth. He offers no identification of the nations at all.

The refrain that follows is handled briefly and warmly. John Gill reports the Targum, which reads the Word of the Lord of hosts, and identifies him as the one whose name is Immanuel, King of kings, who has all creatures in heaven and earth at his command and whom all the hosts of angels obey; he being on the side of his people, they have nothing to fear from the armies of men, since more are they that are for them than they that are against them. Adam Clarke draws the contrast of numbers sharply: the Jews were but a handful of feeble men, but the God of armies was on their side, and none could attack him with hope of success. The second title he takes as a pledge of continuity — the God who appeared to Jacob in his distress and saved him out of all his troubles appeared also for his descendants, and has proved that he has not forgotten his covenant. Charles Ellicott adds only a note on the last word, which he says is rightly given in the margin with the idea of height, as height gives security.
8:
The call to come and look is taken by most as a summons to read history. C.H. Spurgeon pictures the citizens of Jerusalem going forth to view the remains of their enemies and mark the prowess of Jehovah; and he thinks it would be well if we also noted the providential dealings of our covenant God and perceived his hand in the battles of his church. Whenever we read history it should be with this verse sounding in our ears, and the newspaper in the same spirit, to see how the Head of the church rules the nations for his people’s good, as Joseph governed Egypt for Israel. John Gill takes the words as an address of the psalmist to his friends, as Apollinarius supplies it, or of the church to the fearful among them, dismayed at the world’s commotions and encouraged to trust in the Lord from his works. Adam Clarke is brief: see empires destroyed and regenerated in such a way as to show a supernatural agency at work, since God’s hand alone could effect such changes.

What the desolations are is a question of the word itself, and Charles Ellicott offers two senses. The primary meaning is silence, so the phrase may denote the silence of desolation; or, as at Jeremiah 19:8, it may mean wonders, things that silence by their suddenness. The Greek and Latin take it the second way, and he judges the next verse to confirm them. Many manuscripts, he notes, read the divine name in its other form. John Wesley says only that they fall among those who were vexatious to God’s people.

C.H. Spurgeon keeps the desolations literal and presses them further than anyone. The ruined cities of Assyria, Babylon, Petra, Bashan and Canaan are our instructors, recording the doings of the Lord in tables of stone: where his cause and crown have been disregarded ruin has surely followed, sin being a blight on nations that leaves their palaces in heaps. Then he brings it home: the dismantled castles and ruined abbeys of his own land stand as memorials of the Lord’s victories over oppression and superstition — and, he adds, may there soon be more such desolations.

How far the peace of the next verse extends they dispute. John Gill reads it universally and in three stages: a general peace at the birth of Christ the Prince of peace, in the days of Augustus, though it did not last; a cessation from war and persecution under Constantine, signified by the silence in heaven for half an hour; and chiefly the latter day, when nations shall learn war no more and Christ’s kingdom take place. The consideration of it, he adds, may relieve distressed minds under terrible apprehensions of present calamities. John Wesley narrows the same clause to a single country: the land meant is Israel, from one end of it to the other, the bows and spears and chariots broken being their enemies’.

Adam Clarke narrows it differently, to a datable event. God has tranquillised the whole empire by the death of Cambyses and the setting of Darius son of Hystaspes on the Persian throne; the God who delivered us to our enemies for our unfaithfulness has now turned that captivity, and raised us up powerful friends in the very place where we endured so great a fight of afflictions. The disarming he takes as a measure of the quiet: God has rendered useless all the implements of war, and the tranquillity is so secure that the bow may safely be broken, the spear snapped and the chariot burnt. Charles Ellicott adds only a cross-reference to a classical parallel.
10:
Who is told to be still is the question. John Gill reports answers that make it an address to the nations: the Targum renders it cease from war, Jarchi takes it as a command to go up no more against Jerusalem, and Kimchi makes it an exhortation to cease from evil works and know that the Lord is God, who has power to raise up and to make low. Gill himself prefers to keep the speaker where he was, taking the words as a continuation of the church’s address to the fearful among her: as they were bidden before to behold the works of the Lord, so now to hearken to what he says. John Wesley takes the other side without hesitation — stir no more against my people — and glosses the name that follows as the only true and almighty God, over against gods that are but dumb and impotent idols.

Adam Clarke turns the command on the hearers instead, and multiplies it. Cease from your provocations of the divine justice; cease from murmuring against the dispensations of his providence; cease from your labour for a season, that you may deeply reflect on the severity and goodness of God; cease from sin and rebellion, and let that disgrace you no more. The knowledge required he states as broadly: understand that I am the fountain of power, wisdom, justice, goodness and truth.

John Gill is careful about what the stillness is not. It does not mean that they should be like sticks and stones, indolent and unconcerned at the commotions in the earth, unaffected by the judgments of God and wholly inactive; it means that they should not be fearful, fretful or tumultuous, but quiet and resigned to the will of God. Charles Ellicott says nothing of the sense and everything of the effect: the introduction of the divine Protector himself, speaking just before the refrain, is a fine touch of art.

How the exaltation comes about divides the last clause. Adam Clarke makes it two operations on two attributes: by the dispensation of punishments the heathen shall know him to be the God of justice, and by the publication of his gospel the God of goodness; and in the earth he will be exalted by having his salvation proclaimed in every nation and tongue. John Wesley keeps to the works themselves — I will make myself glorious by my great and wonderful works.

The refrain returns unchanged, and they take it as deliberate repetition. John Gill notes the Targum’s Word of the Lord of hosts again, and says the same words are repeated here to comfort those who were fearful and unbelieving, the church comforting herself with them. Adam Clarke hears it as a response: having heard these declarations, the people cry out with joy that the God of armies is with them and they will not fear what man can do; he who saved our fathers will save us and never abandon his people in distress. The Selah he reads as a seal on the whole — this is a firm, lasting, unshaken, well-tried truth.
